title: Level 14: EEPROM Read/Write — Non-Volatile Data Storage
aim: To read and write data to the ATmega328P's built-in 1024-byte EEPROM, demonstrating persistent storage by writing a counter to EEPROM across power cycles and proving data survival without power.
objective: Understand the ATmega328P's EEPROM technology (byte-addressable, 100,000 write endurance cycles), the EEPROM register set (EEARH/L, EEDR, EECR), write timing, the avr/eeprom.h helper library, and wear-levelling considerations for embedded products.
theory:
What is EEPROM?

EEPROM (Electrically Erasable Programmable Read-Only Memory) is a type of non-volatile memory that retains data without power and can be erased and rewritten electrically — byte by byte. Unlike Flash memory (which must be erased in large pages), EEPROM supports individual byte-granular erase and write operations.

ATmega328P EEPROM Specifications

  • Capacity: 1024 bytes (addresses 0x000–0x3FF)
  • Write endurance: 100,000 erase/write cycles minimum per byte
  • Data retention: 20 years at 25°C
  • Self-timed write: Each write cycle takes approximately 3.4 ms — CPU can execute other code after initiating the write
  • Atomic erase+write: Default mode erases and writes in one operation. Separate erase-only and write-only modes are available for faster operation

EEPROM vs Flash vs SRAM

MemoryVolatile?GranularityEnduranceSpeed
SRAMYesByteInfinite1 cycle
FlashNoPage (128B)10,000 cycles~1 ms/page
EEPROMNoByte100,000 cycles3.4 ms/byte

EEPROM Control Registers

  • EEARH:EEARL — EEPROM Address Register (0–1023). Load with target address before any operation.
  • EEDR — EEPROM Data Register. Load with byte to write; contains read byte after a read.
  • EECR — EEPROM Control Register:
    • EERE (bit 0) — Read Enable. Pulse HIGH to read
    • EEPE (bit 1) — Program Enable. Pulse HIGH to program (write)
    • EEMPE (bit 2) — Master Program Enable. Must be set ≤4 cycles before EEPE. Safety interlock prevents accidental writes.
    • EERIE (bit 3) — EEPROM Ready Interrupt Enable
    • EEPM1:EEPM0 (bits 5:4) — Programming Mode: 00=erase+write, 01=erase only, 10=write only

Write Sequence (Critical Timing)

The EEPROM write sequence has strict timing requirements to prevent accidental writes:

  1. Wait for any previous write to complete: while(EECR & (1<<EEPE));
  2. Wait for Flash erase to complete (if any SELFPROGEN): while(SPMCSR & (1<<SELFPROGEN));
  3. Load address into EEAR, data into EEDR
  4. Set EEMPE (Master Program Enable) — enables writing for the next 4 clock cycles
  5. Within 4 cycles: set EEPE to start write. This MUST use cli()/sei() to prevent interrupt from delaying step 5

avr/eeprom.h — Safe Helper Functions

The AVR-libc <avr/eeprom.h> library wraps all the above in safe, tested functions:

  • eeprom_read_byte(addr) — Read 1 byte from EEPROM address (pointer)
  • eeprom_write_byte(addr, val) — Write 1 byte, handles timing internally
  • eeprom_update_byte(addr, val) — Only writes if value differs (saves endurance cycles)
  • eeprom_read_word(addr), eeprom_write_word(addr, val) — 16-bit variants

Wear Levelling

With 100,000 write cycles per byte, writing a counter that increments every second would exhaust one EEPROM cell in 100,000 seconds ≈ 27.8 hours. For frequently changing data, wear levelling distributes writes across multiple addresses. The eeprom_update_byte() function implements a simple optimization: it reads first and only writes if the value has changed, avoiding unnecessary write cycles.

pretest.question: How many bytes of EEPROM does the ATmega328P have?
pretest.explanation: The ATmega328P has exactly 1024 bytes (1 KB) of EEPROM at addresses 0x000–0x3FF.

pretest.question: What is the minimum write endurance per EEPROM byte cell?
pretest.explanation: The ATmega328P datasheet specifies 100,000 erase/write cycles minimum endurance per EEPROM cell. After this, data retention may degrade.

pretest.question: What is the key difference between EEPROM and Flash in terms of erase granularity?
options: EEPROM can be erased byte-by-byte; Flash requires erasing entire pages (128+ bytes)
pretest.explanation: EEPROM supports individual byte erase/write operations. Flash memory is page-based — you must erase an entire page (128 bytes on ATmega328P) before writing any byte in it.

pretest.question: Which register holds the EEPROM address?
pretest.explanation: EEARH (high byte) and EEARL (low byte) together form the 10-bit EEPROM Address Register, addressing locations 0–1023.

pretest.question: Why does the EEPROM write sequence require EEMPE to be set before EEPE?
options: EEMPE is a safety interlock to prevent accidental writes — EEPE only works within 4 cycles of setting EEMPE
pretest.explanation: EEMPE (Master Program Enable) must be set within 4 clock cycles before EEPE (Program Enable). This two-step sequence prevents a runaway program or interrupt from accidentally corrupting EEPROM.

pretest.question: What does eeprom_update_byte() do differently from eeprom_write_byte()?
options: It reads first and only writes if the value differs — preserving endurance cycles
pretest.explanation: eeprom_update_byte() reads the existing value first. If the new value equals the existing, no write is performed. This saves endurance cycles for frequently-updated values that often don't change.

pretest.question: How long does one EEPROM write cycle take?
pretest.explanation: One EEPROM write cycle (erase+program) takes approximately 3.4 ms on the ATmega328P. Multiple back-to-back writes accumulate this delay.

pretest.question: Why must interrupts be disabled between setting EEMPE and EEPE?
options: An interrupt between EEMPE and EEPE could take longer than 4 cycles, expiring the EEMPE window
EEPROM cannot be accessed in ISR
pretest.explanation: EEMPE expires after 4 clock cycles. If an interrupt fires between setting EEMPE and EEPE, and the ISR takes >4 cycles (virtually guaranteed), EEMPE expires and EEPE has no effect — the write is silently lost.

pretest.question: What is wear levelling in EEPROM?
options: Distributing writes across multiple addresses to avoid exhausting any single cell
pretest.explanation: Wear levelling spreads writes across multiple EEPROM addresses using a rotating pointer, ensuring no single cell reaches the endurance limit first.

pretest.question: After a power cycle, what data persists?
options: Flash program code and EEPROM data only
SRAM, Flash, and EEPROM all persist
pretest.explanation: Flash (program code) and EEPROM are non-volatile — they survive power-off. SRAM is volatile and loses all data on power-off or reset.

procedure: Include #include <avr/io.h>, #include <avr/eeprom.h>, and #include <util/delay.h>. Wire a button to PD2 (pull-up) and an LED with 330 Ω to PB5. Optionally wire UART TX for serial output.
Define an EEPROM variable using the avr/eeprom.h declaration syntax: uint8_t EEMEM rebootCount = 0;. The EEMEM attribute places this variable's address in EEPROM space at compile time.
At startup, read the stored boot counter: uint8_t count = eeprom_read_byte(&rebootCount);. If the EEPROM was never written (factory state), it returns 0xFF. Check: if 0xFF, initialise to 0.
Increment the count and write it back: count = (count == 0xFF) ? 1 : count + 1; eeprom_update_byte(&rebootCount, count);. Use eeprom_update_byte to save write cycles if value unchanged.
Display the count via UART: uart_print("Boot count: "); uart_print_num(count); uart_print("\r\n");. Also blink the LED 'count' times so it's visible without a terminal.

Implement the manual EEPROM write sequence (without helper library) to understand low-level access: wait for previous EEPE to clear, disable interrupts (cli), load EEAR with address, EEDR with data, set EEMPE, set EEPE, enable interrupts (sei). This teaches the actual hardware access sequence.

For the read-back test: after writing, perform an immediate read from the same address and verify the value matches what was written. Print 'EEPROM verify OK' or 'EEPROM verify FAIL' based on comparison.
Power cycle the board (unplug and replug USB). Observe that the boot count increments with each power cycle — proving non-volatile storage. After 10 power cycles, count should read 10.

posttest.question: At 1 write per second, how many days before a single EEPROM byte reaches its endurance limit?
posttest.explanation: 100,000 writes / 86,400 seconds per day ≈ 1.157 days. So a byte written every second lasts only about 1.16 days. Wear levelling or write-rate reduction is essential.

posttest.question: What does reading an unused (factory-erased) EEPROM cell return?
posttest.explanation: EEPROM cells in the erased state return 0xFF (all bits set HIGH). This is why firmware must check for 0xFF as an 'uninitialized' sentinel value.

posttest.question: What happens to SRAM on power-off vs EEPROM on power-off?
posttest.explanation: SRAM is volatile — loses data instantly on power-off. EEPROM is non-volatile — data persists without power for up to 20 years.

posttest.question: eeprom_read_byte() takes which type of argument?
posttest.explanation: eeprom_read_byte() takes a pointer to an EEMEM variable, such as &myVar where myVar is declared with EEMEM attribute. This is the EEPROM address, not the byte value.

posttest.question: What is the 'erase-only' mode (EEPM1=0, EEPM0=1) used for?
options: Set a cell to 0xFF without writing — useful if you know the programming step already has the byte set
posttest.explanation: Separate erase-only and write-only modes halve the cycle time (only erase: ~1.8 ms, only write: ~1.8 ms). Useful when you know 0xFF is already written and just need to program 0-bits.

posttest.question: The ATmega328P Flash has 32 KB. How many bytes is that?
posttest.explanation: 32 KB = 32 × 1024 = 32,768 bytes. Flash stores the compiled program (machine code instructions).

posttest.question: What is a watchdog timer used for?
posttest.explanation: WDT auto-resets MCU when not periodically cleared.

posttest.question: Which is NOT a valid ATmega328P port?
posttest.explanation: ATmega328P has Port B, C, D only.

posttest.question: In an ISR, interrupts are automatically:
posttest.explanation: AVR clears I-bit in SREG on ISR entry.

posttest.question: What does the SREG register contain?
posttest.explanation: SREG holds CPU flags (C, Z, N, V, H, S, T) and the global interrupt enable bit (I).

feedback: Remarkable! EEPROM is essential for every product that must remember settings, calibration data, error logs, or serial numbers across power cycles. You now understand how to use it safely, efficiently, and with endurance awareness.
